analysis.one_liner: Sets national limits on formaldehyde emissions from composite wood products like plywood and particleboard.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the bill by unanimous consent on June 14, 2010, the House passed it by voice vote on June 23, and the President signed it on July 7, 2010, making it Public Law 111-199.
analysis.plain_summary: This law writes California's formaldehyde emission limits for hardwood plywood, medium-density fiberboard, and particleboard into federal law, applying them whether the panel is sold bare or built into furniture, cabinets, and other finished goods. The Environmental Protection Agency must set rules covering labeling, testing, third-party certification, recordkeeping, and import checks, and HUD must update its formaldehyde rules for manufactured homes to match. Formaldehyde is a chemical used in wood adhesives, and long-term exposure is a known health risk, so the law aims to lower what families breathe from everyday furniture and building products.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers — families buying furniture, kitchen cabinets, countertops, and manufactured homes made with composite wood — who get reduced exposure to a toxic emission in their own homes. Workers in plants and showrooms who spend their days around these products also benefit from lower ambient levels.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families buying furniture and manufactured homes

how_it_helps.text: Adopts the California formaldehyde emission standard as a national standard for hardwood plywood, medium-density fiberboard, and particleboard sold, supplied, offered for sale, or manufactured in the United States, with listed exemptions [S2].
The standard applies regardless of whether the wood panel is unfinished or already incorporated into a finished good, so protection reaches consumers buying furniture, not just raw panels [S3].

Requires EPA to write implementing regulations covering labeling, chain-of-custody, third-party testing and certification, auditing of certifiers, recordkeeping, and enforcement, and to coordinate with Customs and Border Protection so imported products must meet the same rules [S3].

Requires the HUD Secretary to update the formaldehyde emission controls for plywood and particleboard in manufactured homes within 180 days of EPA's regulations, extending the protection to manufactured housing [S3].
Makes violations a prohibited act under the Toxic Substances Control Act, so companies that break the rules face federal enforcement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Composite wood product makers, furniture and cabinet manufacturers, and importers, who must reformulate resins, pay for quarterly testing and third-party certification, and keep records. Some of that cost can pass to consumers as somewhat higher prices on furniture and building products.

drawbacks.text: The law phases in the strictest limits: higher emission levels were allowed for particleboard and medium-density fiberboard until July 1, 2011, and for hardwood plywood with composite cores and thin fiberboard until July 1, 2012, so exposure continued at higher levels during the phase-in [S4].
Inventory manufactured before a designated date is not subject to the emission standards, so older, non-compliant products already made could keep selling under the sell-through provisions [S3].

The law exempts a long list of products — hardboard, structural plywood and panels, oriented strand board, glued laminated lumber, wood I-joists, wood packaging and pallets, and composite wood inside new vehicles, rail cars, boats, aircraft, and low-content windows and doors — leaving those unregulated [S3].
EPA did not have to issue implementing regulations until January 1, 2013, with import rules due July 1, 2013, so the standards took years to reach store shelves [S4].
Compliance — reformulated resins, quarterly testing, and third-party certification — adds costs for manufacturers, some of which consumers may pay in higher prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a real reduction in a toxic emission in furniture, cabinets, and manufactured homes — products found in most American households — and the cost is compliance spending by manufacturers and modestly higher prices for consumers. The phase-in delays and sell-through allowances soften the immediate benefit, and the exemption list leaves some products unregulated, but the core protection applies to the products families actually live with and covers imports equally, so the benefit is broad and the cost is moderate.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it by unanimous consent, the House passed it by voice vote under a procedure reserved for non-controversial bills, and the President signed it nine days after House passage.

narrative.text: Introduced in the Senate on September 10, 2009, and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S6].
The committee ordered it reported favorably with a substitute amendment in December 2009 and reported it in April 2010 with written report No. 111-169 [S6].
Passed the Senate by unanimous consent on June 14, 2010, with the committee substitute agreed to by unanimous consent [S6].
Passed the House on June 23, 2010, on a motion to suspend the rules and pass the bill, agreed to by voice vote, and was signed by the President on July 7, 2010, becoming Public Law 111-199 [S6].
The law's emission limits phase in over several years and EPA's implementing regulations were due by January 1, 2013, so the standards took effect over time rather than immediately [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers, who gained a federal limit on formaldehyde in furniture and manufactured homes; manufacturers absorbed compliance costs but got one national standard instead of a state-by-state patchwork.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers, plus manufacturers who got one national standard

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: 10 of 40 Senate Republicans joined 8 of 58 Senate Democrats and the lone Independent as cosponsors, and the bill passed the Senate by unanimous consent and the House by voice vote with no recorded opposition [S5] [S6].

industries.industry: Composite wood product manufacturers (hardwood plywood, particleboard, medium-density fiberboard)
industries.note: They must reformulate resins, run quarterly emission tests, and pay for third-party certification, which costs money. In exchange they get one national standard replacing a patchwork of state rules, with the same limits applying to imports [S3].

industries.industry: Furniture, cabinet, and countertop makers using composite wood
industries.note: They must source compliant panels and manage labeling and recordkeeping for finished goods, raising costs. Their customers get safer products, so their interest in a credible standard runs alongside the public's [S3].
The law mandates third-party testing, certification, and auditing of certifiers, creating new required business for accredited labs and certifiers [S3].

industries.industry: Importers of foreign-made composite wood products
industries.note: EPA must revise import certification rules with Customs and Border Protection by July 1, 2013, so foreign panels and finished goods must meet the same emission limits, ending a price advantage from lower-emission alternatives abroad [S3].
